question: Under OREC rules, by when must a broker deposit escrow funds received in connection with a real estate transaction, absent a different written agreement of the parties?
choice_a: By the end of the same banking day the funds are received
choice_b: By the end of the third banking day following acceptance of an offer or receipt of the escrow funds
choice_c: Within ten calendar days of receipt
choice_d: Before the next Commission audit cycle
explanation: OAC 605:10-13-1(a)(1)(D) requires all escrow funds to be deposited before the end of the third banking day following acceptance of an offer by an offeree or receipt of the escrow funds, unless otherwise agreed to in writing by all interested parties.

question: Who must be a signatory on a brokerage's trust or escrow account under OREC rules?
choice_a: Any licensed associate affiliated with the firm
choice_b: The financial institution's branch manager
choice_c: The broker
choice_d: The OREC executive director
explanation: OAC 605:10-13-1(a)(1)(B) requires the broker to be a signor on any brokerage account where trust/escrow funds are held.

question: How must an Oklahoma broker's trust or escrow account be titled?
choice_a: In the name of the individual buyer or seller in the pending transaction
choice_b: As a generic "operating account" indistinguishable from other firm accounts
choice_c: In the name of the title company handling the closing
choice_d: In the name of the broker or brokerage as it appears on the license or registered trade name, styled as a trust or escrow account
explanation: OAC 605:10-13-1(a)(1)(C) requires the account to be in the name of the broker or brokerage as it appears on the license or trade name registered with the Commission, and styled as a trust or escrow account.

question: What personal funds, if any, may an Oklahoma broker keep in the trust account?
choice_a: Only an amount sufficient to maintain the account's integrity and cover financial institution servicing charges
choice_b: Up to $5,000 of the broker's own operating capital
choice_c: Any amount, as long as it is tracked in a separate ledger
choice_d: None whatsoever, under any circumstance
explanation: OAC 605:10-13-1(b) prohibits commingling but permits the broker to keep in the trust account amounts sufficient to insure the integrity of the account and cover charges made by the financial institution for servicing it.

question: Under the Oklahoma Real Estate License Code's grounds for discipline, commingling is defined as keeping the licensee's own money or property together with money or property of others EXCEPT in which circumstance?
choice_a: When the combined amount is under $500
choice_b: When the money or property of others is received and held in an escrow account that contains only money or property of others
choice_c: When the licensee discloses the commingling in the closing statement
choice_d: When the funds are held for fewer than three banking days
explanation: 59 O.S. § 858-312(16) lists commingling as a ground for discipline, with the express exception for money or property of others held in an escrow account containing only money or property of others.

question: May an Oklahoma broker place escrow monies in an interest-bearing account?
choice_a: No, escrow accounts must always be non-interest-bearing
choice_b: Yes, but only with prior written approval of the Oklahoma Real Estate Commission for each transaction
choice_c: Yes, but the broker must disclose in writing to all parties that the account bears interest and identify who receives the interest
choice_d: Yes, and the broker is automatically entitled to keep all interest without disclosure
explanation: OAC 605:10-13-1(c) permits interest-bearing escrow accounts if the broker discloses in writing to all parties that the account bears interest and identifies the party receiving the interest; the Commission does not prohibit the broker from receiving the earned interest if disclosed.

question: What type of interest-bearing account is a broker permitted to use for escrow funds in Oklahoma?
choice_a: Any account type, including certificates of deposit
choice_b: A money market account held out of state
choice_c: Only a non-federally-insured account offering the highest available rate
choice_d: A demand-type account only; certificates of deposit and other time deposits are prohibited
explanation: OAC 605:10-13-1(c) requires that an interest-bearing escrow account be a demand-type account, which prohibits the use of certificates of deposit or other time deposits as trust/escrow accounts.

question: When is an Oklahoma broker required to maintain a trust or escrow account?
choice_a: Only when the broker accepts monies or other depositable items belonging to others
choice_b: At all times, regardless of whether the broker ever holds client funds
choice_c: Only after the broker's first three closed transactions
choice_d: Only for commercial transactions, never residential
explanation: OAC 605:10-13-1(d) provides that a broker is not required to maintain a trust or escrow account unless monies or other depositable items belonging to others are accepted and require placement in the broker's trust account.

question: What must an Oklahoma broker do regarding trust and escrow accounts with respect to the Commission?
choice_a: Only report the accounts during a biennial license renewal survey
choice_b: Notify the Commission in writing of all trust or escrow, security deposit, rental management, and interest-bearing accounts holding trust funds, and notify the Commission in writing when any such account is closed
choice_c: Report account balances to the Commission verbally at the annual convention
choice_d: Nothing; trust account registration with OREC is optional
explanation: OAC 605:10-13-1(e) requires a broker to notify the Commission in writing of all trust or escrow accounts, security deposit accounts, rental management operating accounts, and interest-bearing accounts holding trust funds, and to inform the Commission in writing when any such account is closed.

question: What is the significance of a broker failing to pay over trust funds within three days after closing of a transaction?
choice_a: It is automatically excused if the delay is less than two weeks
choice_b: It only matters if the buyer files a civil lawsuit first
choice_c: It constitutes prima facie evidence of a violation in any license suspension or revocation hearing
choice_d: It has no regulatory consequence as long as funds are eventually disbursed
explanation: OAC 605:10-13-1(g) requires a broker to pay over all sums held promptly after closing, and provides that failure to pay over such sums within three days after closing is prima facie evidence of a violation in a suspension or revocation hearing.

question: If a real estate transaction fails to consummate, what must the broker do with the earnest money held in escrow?
choice_a: Retain it in the trust account indefinitely until requested by either party
choice_b: Automatically forward it to the Oklahoma Real Estate Education and Recovery Fund
choice_c: Split it evenly between buyer and seller regardless of the contract terms
choice_d: Promptly disburse it to the proper party in accordance with the terms of the contract, or follow the special escrow disbursement rule if a dispute arises
explanation: OAC 605:10-13-1(h) requires a broker to promptly disburse earnest money or items to the proper party per the contract terms if a transaction does not consummate; if a dispute arises before disbursement, the broker follows OAC 605:10-13-3 or may file an interpleader action.

question: What bookkeeping is an Oklahoma broker required to maintain for trust account compliance?
choice_a: A system such as canceled checks, a checkbook, deposit receipts, and a general accounts ledger that accurately and clearly discloses full compliance with trust account law
choice_b: No specific bookkeeping system is mandated as long as taxes are filed correctly
choice_c: Only a single annual summary statement submitted to the Commission
choice_d: A verbal log kept by the broker's assistant
explanation: OAC 605:10-13-1(k) requires a broker to maintain a bookkeeping system (e.g., canceled checks, checkbook, deposit receipts, general accounts ledger) that accurately and clearly discloses full compliance with trust account requirements.

question: How long must an Oklahoma broker retain trust account records, and from what date does that period begin?
choice_a: Two years, beginning with the date the transaction contract was signed
choice_b: Five years, beginning with the date of disbursal of funds
choice_c: One year, beginning with the date of closing
choice_d: Trust account records need not be retained once the transaction closes
explanation: OAC 605:10-13-1(l) requires records to be maintained for a minimum of five years after consummation or termination of a transaction; for trust account records specifically, the five-year period commences with the date of disbursal of funds.

question: If a broker wants to move trust account records to alternative (electronic) media, how long must those records first be kept in their original format?
choice_a: They may be converted to alternative media immediately upon creation
choice_b: A minimum of four years
choice_c: A minimum of two years, before transfer to alternative media for the remainder of the retention period
choice_d: Original-format retention is not required for trust account records
explanation: OAC 605:10-13-1(m)(1) requires trust account records to be maintained by the broker in their original format for a minimum of two years before they may be transferred to alternative media for the remaining required retention time.

question: May a real estate associate (not a broker) in Oklahoma open or be a signer on a trust or escrow account?
choice_a: Yes, any associate may freely open and sign on trust accounts
choice_b: Only associates with more than five years of experience may do so
choice_c: Only if the managing broker is unavailable for more than 30 days
choice_d: No, not while providing licensed real estate activities, except when the associate is performing activities on their own behalf as outlined in the personal-transaction provisions of the Code
explanation: OAC 605:10-13-2(3) provides that an associate shall not be authorized to open or maintain a trust or escrow account, or be a signer on one, while providing licensed activities; an exception exists only when the associate is performing activities under Section 858-301 of the Code (e.g., regarding the associate's own property).

question: Under OREC's special escrow disbursement rule, what must a broker do if a dispute arises before disbursement of escrowed money or valuables?
choice_a: Continue to retain the money or valuables in escrow until receiving a written release from all parties consenting to its disposition, or until a civil action is filed and the funds are paid into court
choice_b: Immediately disburse the funds to whichever party demands them first
choice_c: Return the funds to the brokerage's operating account pending resolution
choice_d: Automatically forward the disputed funds to the Recovery Fund
explanation: OAC 605:10-13-3(a) requires the broker to retain disputed escrow money or valuables until a written release is obtained from all parties, or until a civil action is filed, at which point the broker may pay or turn the funds into court.

question: Absent a pending civil action, when may a broker disburse disputed escrow funds based on a good-faith determination that one party failed to perform, and what notice is required?
choice_a: Immediately, with no notice required
choice_b: After 30 days from the date of final termination of the contract, and only after giving 15 days' written notice to all parties concerned
choice_c: After 90 days, with no notice required
choice_d: After 10 days, with 30 days' notice required
explanation: OAC 605:10-13-3(b) allows disbursement, without it being grounds for discipline, after 30 days from final termination of the contract based on a good-faith decision by the broker, provided 15 days' written notice of the proposed action is given to all parties.

question: Under the Oklahoma Real Estate License Code, failing within a reasonable time to account for or remit monies belonging to others that come into a licensee's possession is treated as what?
choice_a: A minor clerical issue with no regulatory consequence
choice_b: Grounds for discipline only if the amount exceeds $10,000
choice_c: A statutory ground for disciplinary action against the licensee
choice_d: A matter handled exclusively through small claims court, never by the Commission
explanation: 59 O.S. § 858-312(6) lists failing, within a reasonable time, to account for or remit any monies, documents, or other property belonging to others as a statutory ground for disciplinary action.

question: Under OREC's disciplinary rules, failing to maintain trust account documents for the retention period required by rule is treated as what?
choice_a: Only relevant if a consumer complaint is also filed
choice_b: Not a disciplinary matter, only a bookkeeping best practice
choice_c: Grounds for discipline only against associates, never brokers
choice_d: An independent, specifically enumerated ground for disciplinary action
explanation: OAC 605:10-17-4 lists, among enumerated grounds for discipline, failing to maintain documents relating to a trust account or real estate transaction for the time period required by Rule 605:10-13-1.

question: What is the Oklahoma Real Estate Education and Recovery Fund, as created by statute?
choice_a: A continuing revolving fund in the State Treasury, administered by the Oklahoma Real Estate Commission and funded by dedicated licensee fees, not subject to fiscal year limitations
choice_b: A private insurance policy each broker must purchase individually
choice_c: A one-time state appropriation that expires after five years
choice_d: A federal fund administered by HUD on Oklahoma's behalf
explanation: 59 O.S. § 858-601(A) creates the Oklahoma Real Estate Education and Recovery Fund as a continuing revolving fund in the State Treasury, administered by OREC and funded by fees assessed under the Code, not subject to fiscal year limitations.

question: What additional fee is added to an Oklahoma real estate license fee (original or renewal) to fund the Education and Recovery Fund?
choice_a: $100.00 for every license, with no exceptions
choice_b: $20.00, except a provisional sales associate pays $15.00 for the twelve-month provisional term
choice_c: 1% of the licensee's prior-year commission income
choice_d: There is no separate Recovery Fund fee; it is funded solely by fines
explanation: Under the OREC fee schedule (OAC 605), a $20.00 Education and Recovery Fund fee is added to and payable with the license fee for an original license and each renewal, except a provisional sales associate's fee is $15.00 for the twelve-month provisional term.
source_note: OAC 605 fee schedule (Recovery Fund fee); 59 O.S. § 858-602

question: What is one condition a claimant must satisfy to be eligible to seek recovery from the Oklahoma Real Estate Education and Recovery Fund?
choice_a: The claimant must have first exhausted a private title insurance claim
choice_b: The claimant must be a licensed real estate broker themselves
choice_c: The claimant's cause of action must have accrued not more than two years prior to filing the district court action, and the Commission must be notified in writing at the commencement of the action
choice_d: The claim must be filed directly with the Commission with no court action required
explanation: 59 O.S. § 858-603(A) requires, among other conditions, that the cause of action accrued not more than two years prior to filing suit, and that the Commission be notified in writing at the commencement of the action with a file-stamped copy of the petition.

question: Which of the following claimants is statutorily ineligible to recover from the Oklahoma Real Estate Education and Recovery Fund?
choice_a: A buyer who purchased a home through a licensed broker
choice_b: A seller who received a below-market offer
choice_c: A tenant who paid a security deposit through a property management brokerage
choice_d: A licensee who acted in their own behalf in the transaction that is the subject of the claim
explanation: 59 O.S. § 858-603(B) disqualifies certain claimants, including a licensee who acted in their own behalf in the transaction underlying the claim, the spouse of the judgment debtor, and a claimant jointly responsible for the resulting loss.

question: What is the maximum amount a single claimant may recover from the Oklahoma Real Estate Education and Recovery Fund on an unsatisfied judgment?
choice_a: An amount equal to the unsatisfied portion of the judgment for actual or compensatory damages, or $25,000, whichever is less
choice_b: The full unsatisfied judgment amount with no cap
choice_c: A flat $10,000 regardless of the judgment amount
choice_d: $100,000 per claimant
explanation: 59 O.S. § 858-604(A) caps recovery for a single claimant at the unsatisfied portion of the judgment for actual or compensatory damages, or $25,000, whichever is less.

question: May a successful Recovery Fund claimant be reimbursed for attorney fees, and if so, subject to what limit?
choice_a: Yes, attorney fees are reimbursed in full with no cap
choice_b: Yes, reasonably incurred attorney fees may be reimbursed up to 25% of the amount approved by the Commission; court costs and other expenses are not recoverable
choice_c: No, attorney fees are never reimbursable from the fund
choice_d: Yes, but only up to a flat $500 regardless of the claim size
explanation: 59 O.S. § 858-604(A) allows reimbursement of reasonably incurred attorney fees up to 25% of the claimant's Commission-approved amount, documented and verified, while stating that court costs and other expenses are not recoverable from the fund.

question: What is the maximum aggregate amount the Oklahoma Real Estate Education and Recovery Fund will pay for claims arising out of the same transaction, regardless of the number of claimants or parcels involved?
choice_d: There is no aggregate limit per transaction, only a per-claimant limit
explanation: 59 O.S. § 858-604(C) limits payments for claims arising out of the same transaction to an aggregate of $50,000, irrespective of the number of claimants or parcels of real estate involved.

question: What is the maximum aggregate amount the Recovery Fund will pay out on judgments against any one licensee?
choice_c: There is no per-licensee aggregate cap, only a per-transaction cap
explanation: 59 O.S. § 858-604(D) provides that payments for claims based on judgments against any one licensee shall not exceed an aggregate of $50,000.

question: If the Recovery Fund has insufficient money to satisfy a valid claim, what special levy may the Commission collect from licensees, and how often?
choice_a: A special levy of up to $5.00 per licensee, collected not more than once each fiscal year
choice_b: A mandatory levy of $100 per licensee, collected monthly
choice_c: A one-time levy of $1,000 collected only from brokers, never associates
choice_d: No additional levy is ever permitted; unpaid claims are simply denied
explanation: 59 O.S. § 858-604(E) authorizes the Commission to collect a special levy from fund members not to exceed $5.00 each fiscal year if fund monies are insufficient to satisfy a valid claim, with outstanding claims paid in the order approved once funds become available.

question: What happens to a licensee's license when the Recovery Fund pays a claim on a judgment against that licensee?
choice_a: Nothing changes; the licensee keeps practicing without restriction
choice_b: The license is automatically revoked, and cannot be reinstated until the licensee repays the fund in full plus 7% annual interest
choice_c: The license is suspended for a fixed 90 days regardless of repayment
choice_d: The license converts to inactive status until the next renewal cycle
explanation: 59 O.S. § 858-604(G) provides that the license is automatically revoked upon payment from the fund on a judgment against the licensee, and reinstatement is barred until the licensee repays the fund in full, plus interest at 7% per year, for the amount paid.

question: A claim is made against a licensed brokerage organized as a partnership. To whom is the claim imputed for Recovery Fund purposes?
choice_a: To every associate who ever worked for the partnership, regardless of involvement
choice_b: To the Oklahoma Real Estate Commission itself
choice_c: To the managing broker(s) at the time the cause of action arose
choice_d: To the partnership's registered agent for service of process only, with no license consequence
explanation: 59 O.S. § 858-604(F) provides that any claim against a corporation, association, or partnership is imputed to the managing broker(s) at the time the cause of action arose.

question: Once the Recovery Fund balance exceeds what threshold may the Commission, at its discretion, spend the excess on real estate education purposes for the fiscal year?
explanation: 59 O.S. § 858-605 allows the Commission, in its discretion, to expend excess Recovery Fund monies each fiscal year for education-related purposes once the total deposited in the fund exceeds $250,000.
